content.text: Clues and hints to help you solve puzzle #1029 Updated: Apr 5, 2026 11:00 am WePC is reader-supported. When you buy through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Prices subject to change. Learn more Stuck on today’s NYT Connections puzzle? You’re in the right place. With 16 words to sort into four groups—and only a handful of mistakes allowed—it’s easy to second-guess your choices. The tricky part is that many words seem to fit multiple themes at once. That overlap can throw you off, but this guide will help you narrow things down with hints and, if needed, the full answers. This guide covers NYT Connections puzzle #1029, released on April 5. Hints for today’s Connections groups Here are four clues to help you find the correct groupings. They go from easiest to hardest: 🟨 hint: basic physics terms 🟩 hint: classic detective look 🟦 hint: actions that involve turning something over 🟪 hint: words that begin with terms for wet, messy matter If you’d like an extra nudge, here’s one word from each group: 🟨: ELECTRON 🟩: PIPE 🟦: COIN 🟪: MUSHROOM Today’s Connections answers (April 5) If you’re ready for the full solution, here it is: 🟨 Atomic structure terms: ELECTRON, NUCLEUS, ORBIT, SHELL 🟩 Parts of a Sherlock Holmes costume: DEERSTALKER, MAGNIFYING GLASS, PIPE, VIOLIN 🟦 Things to flip: COIN, LIGHT SWITCH, PANCAKE, THE BIRD 🟪 Starting with synonyms for “slush”: GOOGOL, MUSHROOM, PASTEURIZE, PULPIT Today’s puzzle lands in the medium-to-hard range. The yellow group was fairly direct if you recognized basic science terms, while the green group required some familiarity with classic detective imagery. The blue group was straightforward once you focused on actions rather than objects. The purple group was the toughest, relying on wordplay and spotting hidden prefixes, which made it easy to overlook at first. Does Connections get harder every day? Connections doesn’t steadily increase in difficulty. Some days are easier, while others lean heavily on wordplay or niche knowledge. Each puzzle mixes things up with different themes like definitions, cultural references, or clever twists. Solving one or two groups early can make the rest much easier—but remember, you only get four mistakes before the game ends.
